3. The appeals before the District Judge having common facts and the same question of law were heard together and disposed of by one judgment. But the Controller of Insurance has preferred his separate appeals against the Order of the District Judge before this Court. In this Court too, both the appeals have been heard together and are disposed of by this judgment. 

 10. Before proceeding to consider the appeals on merits it is necessary to dispose of the two preliminary injectors raised by Mr. M.H. Khandkar. As regards the first point, Mr. Khandkar contends that the period of limitation prescribed for preferring an appeal to the High Court against any judgment of any Subordinate Court is ninety days plus the period which is spent for taking copies of the judgment and order. In the instant case the order was passed by the District Judge on 6-10-72 while the appeals were presented on 22-2-73. It appears that for certified copy of the judgment and order application was filed on 27-1-73 and the certified copies were received on 30-1-73. It thus appears that a period of four days was spent in obtaining certified copies of the judgment and order ninety days plus 4 days, i.e. 94 days were available to the appellant to file the appeal before this Court. But the appeal was filed 119 days after the date of judgment and order passed by the District Judge. Hence the appeases out of time by 25 days. 

 11. On the other hand, the learned Additional Attorney General argues that a period of four months from the date on which the order appealed against was passed would be available to the appellants to prefer an appeal to this Court under sub section (4) of section 110 of the Insurance Act. So the appeals are well in time. But Mr. Khandaker contends that this period of four months is prescribed as the period of limitation for preferring the appeal before the District Judge against an order of the Controller of Insurance This period of four months is not available for preferring an appeal to this court against the judgment and order of the District Judge. Except the mere contention that the period of four mouths could not be available to an appellant preferring an appeal before the High Court Division from an order of the District Judge no authority could be cited by Mr Khandaker. Two forums for appeal have been provided under section 110 of the Insurance Act. Subsection (2) of section 110 lays down the forum where the appeal provided for in several clauses if subsection (2) will lie the appeal under this sub-section shall lie to the principle Court of Civil Jurisdiction within whose local limits the principal place of business of the insurer concerned is situate. In other words, the sites of the principal place of business of the insurer determine the form of appeal from the original order and this appeal is popularly known as the first appeal. This appellate forum is the Court of the District Judge. The law also provides an appeal to the High, Court Division from an order of the District Judge. This appeal is ordinarily said to be the second appeal. With, regard to the appeal from the order of the District Judge, subsection (3) of section 110 lays down that an appeal shall lie from any order under subsection (1) to the authority authorized to hear appeals from the decisions of the Court making the same. The said authority, it is not disputed, is this Court that is High Court Division. The period of limitation for an appeal to the District Judge from an original order, that is from the order of the Controller of Insurance and for an appeal from the order of the District Judge to the High Court Division is the same as provided in section 110 (4) of the Insurance Act and this period of limitation is available for both the appeals, i e. the first appeal before the District Judge from the order of the Controller of Insurance and the second appeal before the High Court Division from the order of the District Judge. The said period is four months fiat the date on which tea order appealed against was communicated to the appellant Subsection (4) of section 110 of the Insurance act cannot therefore, be construed to cove rely the first appeal before the District Judge under sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 110 of the said Act. So, the ordinary period of limitation provided in the Limitation Act for as appeal to the High Court Division being ninety days will not apply to the appeals under him Insurance Act which is a special Act and has provided special limitation fur preferring appeals. So, the appeals having been filed within four months from the date of the judgment and order passed by the learned District Judge are well within time. The first objection of Mr. Khandaker regarding limitation fails. 

 12. The second objection urged by Mr. Khandaker is that the preset appeals are it competent because appeal to High Court Division from the order of the District Judge will lie only when the orders passed him are final, that is, if by his order the District Judge finally disposes matter in dispute. But in the instant case the order passed by the learned District Judge is not a final order inasmuch as the learned District Judge did not finally dispose of the dispute between the parties. By his order the District Judge has referred back the dispute to the Controller of Insurance with direction give proper notice in writing to the Companies and to decide the question of registration and grant of certificate of registration in accordance with law. On this point Mr. Khandaker his relied on some decisions, namely 37 C.W N. 405 (V.M Abdul Rahman Vs. D. K. Cassim & Sons and another), A.I R. 1962 Calcutta 417 (Dilip Kumar Ghose Vs. State) and 38 C.W.N. 1083 (Mir Abi Mahammad Minn Vs. Abu Nasar Mahammad Eusuf Ali and others). In the case reported in 37 C.N.W. 405 the question arose as to what was meant by the expression final order under section 109 C.P.C. it has been held by the Privy Council that an order is not a final order within the meaning of section 109 (a) of the Code of Civil Procedure merely because it decided a vital question going to the rout of the suit such as the jurisdiction of the Court to entertain the suit. The finality us, be a finality is relation to the suit. If, after the order, the suit is still a live suit in which the rights of the parties have still to be determined, no appeal lies against it under section 109 (a) C.P.C. It is obvious that this case is not at all at acted to the case under our Consideration. Because in the case under reference the only question which was decided, was with respect to the jurisdiction of the Court, i.e. the competence of the Court to entertain the suit. The decision had nothing to do with the merits of the case and the said decision did not dispose of the point at issue in that suit. In the ease reported in A.I.R. 1962 Calcutta 417 it has been held that the test whether a judgment or an order is final or not is the final determination of the proceeding. In this case the High Court set aside the older of acquittal of the accused and directed a retrial. So, the effect of the was not the termination of the case slatted against the accused but its revival. Such an order keeps alive the case and cannot be said to be a final order. In view of the facts involved in that case, it is also not attracted to the case before us. The last case referred to on this point is the case reported in 38 C.W.N.1083. It was a case under the Guardians and Wards Act. In that case an order was passed refusing the application of a particular application to be appointed guardian of the properties of a minor while the proceedings were kept pending with a view to appointing the Court or Wards or some other suitable party to be guardian. It was held that the order was an interlocutory order and not a final order refusing to appoint a guardian made under section 7 of the Guardians and Wards Act from which an appeal would lie under section 47 (a) of the said Act. 

 "An appeal shall lie from any order made under sub section (1) to the authority authorized to hear appeal from the decisions of the Court making the same and the decision on such appeal shall be final." 

 Mr. Abdus Subhan, learned Advocate for the respondent makes a prayer before us to take hack the rappers and original documents which were flee in Court and sought to be included in the paper book after submitting the certified copies thereof in Court. The prayer is allowed.
